title: Convergence Rate of the Last Iterate of Stochastic Proximal Algorithms
claim: The last iterate of the stochastic proximal method converges faster in practice than the averaged iterate, across synthetic and real data.
layout: 2 side-by-side line plots, semilog y-axis, shared blue-vs-orange curves, shaded variance bands
description: Two side-by-side semilog line plots of objective gap against iteration, from 0 to 10,000. Panel (a) is a synthetic Lasso problem with the gap H(x_t) - H* on the y-axis. Panel (b) is MNIST logistic regression, with the gap measured to a reference solution. Each panel shows two curves: a blue 'Last (mean)' curve and an orange 'Avg (mean)' curve. Both start at the same high value and fall quickly. The blue last-iterate curve falls clearly below the orange averaged curve throughout. Light shaded bands show variation across trials, and they are visibly wider on the noisier MNIST blue curve. Panels have gray gridlines, legends in the upper right, and subcaptions (a) and (b) below. The eye goes first to the gap between the blue and orange curves.
caption: Comparison of last and averaged iterates.
abstract: We analyze two classical algorithms for solving additively composite convex optimization problems where the objective is the sum of a smooth term and a nonsmooth regularizer. The first algorithm is the proximal stochastic gradient method for a single regularizer; the second is the randomized incremental proximal method, which uses the proximal operator of a randomly selected function when the regularizer is given as the sum of many nonsmooth functions. We focus on relaxing the bounded variance assumption that is common, yet stringent, for getting last iterate convergence rates. We prove the $\widetilde{O}(1/\sqrt{T})$ rate of convergence for the last iterate of both algorithms under componentwise convexity and smoothness, which is optimal up to log terms. Our results apply directly to graph-guided regularizers that arise in multi-task and federated learning, where the regularizer decomposes as a sum over edges of a collaboration graph.
